title: STORM: Synergistic Cross-Scale Spatio-Temporal Modeling for Weather Forecasting
claim: Prior models forecast one step at a time from a single view; ours uses multi-scale views to forecast many steps jointly.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, center coarse/fine scale column, feature list at right
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a), "Weather Model", shows a mainstream approach. A single initial-condition global map feeds a blue "Spatial En&Decode" box. This outputs forecast maps for Δt, 2Δt and 3Δt, one step per turn, with dashed arrows and a looping arrow indicating autoregressive feedback. A red arrow points left from the center, labeled "Single-view of Earth". The center column shows a coarse-scale map and a fine-scale map, with two globes between them. Panel (b), "Our STORM", shows stacked maps at Δt to 4Δt entering a "Multi-view Spatial Learn" block. That block feeds a "Temporal Evolution Capture" block, which produces multi-step forecasts for 5Δt to 8Δt. The right edge lists four benefits, each with a colored icon: multi-scale spatial correlation, lightweight temporal encoding, mid- and long-term forecasting, and global and regional adaptability. Weather heatmaps in red and blue draw the eye first.
caption: Comparison of main stream weather forecasting model and our STORM.
abstract: Accurate weather forecasting is crucial for climate research, disaster mitigation, and societal planning. Despite recent progress with deep learning, global atmospheric data remain uniquely challenging since weather dynamics evolve across heterogeneous spatial and temporal scales ranging from planetary circulations to localized phenomena. Capturing such cross-scale interactions within a unified framework remains an open problem. To address this gap, we propose \textbf{STORM}, a spatio-temporal model that disentangles atmospheric variations into multiple scales to uncover scale-specific dependencies. In addition, it enables coherent forecasting across multiple resolutions, maintaining consistent temporal evolution. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that STORM consistently delivers superior performance across both global and regional settings, as well as for short- and long-term forecasts.
